Rudolf Kálmán, un ingeniero nacido en Bu: Rudolf Kálmán, an engineer born in Budapest in 1930 who emigrated to the United States, published the filter in 1960. At first many engineers distrusted it. One of the first to see its reach was Stanley Schmidt, of NASA's Ames centre, who was looking for a way to estimate the trajectory of a spacecraft towards the Moon with scarce measurements and a tiny onboard computer. He adapted it to the problem and the filter ended up flying in the navigation computers of the Apollo programme. It has not stopped flying since.

Toda la idea descansa en la [[pe-normal|: The whole idea rests on the [[pe-normal|normal distribution]]. The prediction is not a number but a bell curve: a central value $x_p$ and a standard deviation $\sigma_p$ saying how far off it may be. The measurement is another bell curve, centred on the measured value $z$ and with deviation $\sigma_m$, the sensor's. If the two pieces of information are independent, the best combined estimate is another bell curve, narrower than both.
